{{Short description|Non-linear partial differential equation}}
: ''For Liouville's equation in differential geometry, see [[Liouville's equation]].''
{{technical|date=May 2025}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Liouville–Bratu–Gelfand equation''' or '''Liouville's equation'''  is a non-linear [[Poisson equation]], named after the mathematicians [[Joseph Liouville]],<ref>Liouville, J. "Sur l’équation aux différences partielles <math>\frac{d^2\log\lambda}{dudv}\pm \frac{\lambda}{2a^2}= 0</math>." Journal de mathématiques pures et appliquées (1853): 71–72. http://sites.mathdoc.fr/JMPA/PDF/JMPA_1853_1_18_A3_0.pdf</ref> Gheorghe Bratu<ref>Bratu, G. "Sur les équations intégrales non linéaires." Bulletin de la Société Mathématique de France 42 (1914): 113–142.http://archive.numdam.org/article/BSMF_1914__42__113_0.pdf</ref> and [[Israel Gelfand]].<ref>Gelfand, I. M. "Some problems in the theory of quasilinear equations." Amer. Math. Soc. Transl 29.2 (1963): 295–381. http://www.mathnet.ru/links/aa75c5d339030f17940afb64e17793d8/rm7290.pdf</ref> The equation reads

:<math>\nabla^2 \psi + \lambda e^\psi = 0</math>

The equation appears in [[thermal runaway]] as [[Frank-Kamenetskii theory]], [[astrophysics]] for example, [[Emden–Chandrasekhar equation]]. This equation also describes [[space charge]] of electricity around a glowing wire<ref>Richardson, Owen Willans. The emission of electricity from hot bodies. Longmans, Green and Company, 1921.</ref> and describes [[planetary nebula]].

==Liouville's solution==
Source:<ref>Bateman, Harry. "Partial differential equations of mathematical physics." Partial Differential Equations of Mathematical Physics, by H. Bateman, Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 1932 (1932).</ref>

In two dimension with [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian Coordinates]] <math>(x,y)</math>, [[Joseph Liouville]] proposed a solution in 1853 as

:<math>\lambda e^\psi (u^2 + v^2 + 1) ^2 = 2 \left[\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)^2\right]</math>

where <math>f(z)=u + i v</math> is an arbitrary [[analytic function]] with <math>z=x+iy</math>. In 1915, G.W. Walker<ref>Walker, George W. "Some problems illustrating the forms of nebulae." Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Containing Papers of a Mathematical and Physical Character 91.631 (1915): 410-420.https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/93512.pdf?refreqid=excelsior%3Af4a4cc9656b8bbd9266f9d32587d02b1</ref> found a solution by assuming a form for <math>f(z)</math>. If <math>r^2=x^2+y^2</math>, then Walker's solution is

:<math>8 e^{-\psi} = \lambda \left[\left(\frac{r}{a}\right)^n + \left(\frac{a}{r}\right)^n\right]^2</math>

where <math>a</math> is some finite radius. This solution decays at infinity for any <math>n</math>, but becomes infinite at the origin for <math>n<1</math> , becomes finite at the origin for <math>n=1</math> and becomes zero at the origin for <math>n>1</math>. Walker also proposed two more solutions in his 1915 paper.

==Radially symmetric forms==

If the system to be studied is radially symmetric, then the equation in <math>n</math> dimension becomes

:<math>\psi'' + \frac{n-1}{r}\psi' + \lambda e^\psi=0</math>

where <math>r</math> is the distance from the origin. With the boundary conditions

:<math>\psi'(0)=0, \quad \psi(1) = 0</math>

and for <math>\lambda\geq 0</math>, a real solution exists only for <math>\lambda \in [0,\lambda_c]</math>, where <math>\lambda_c</math> is the critical parameter called as [[Frank-Kamenetskii theory|'''Frank-Kamenetskii parameter''']]. The critical parameter is <math>\lambda_c=0.8785</math> for <math>n=1</math>, <math>\lambda_c=2</math> for <math>n=2</math> and <math>\lambda_c=3.32</math> for <math>n=3</math>. For <math>n=1, \ 2</math>, two solution exists and for <math>3\leq n\leq 9</math> infinitely many solution exists with solutions oscillating about the point <math>\lambda=2(n-2)</math>. For <math>n\geq 10</math>, the solution is unique and in these cases the critical parameter is given by <math>\lambda_c=2(n-2)</math>. Multiplicity of solution for <math>n=3</math> was discovered by [[Israel Gelfand]] in 1963 and in later 1973 generalized for all <math>n</math> by [[Daniel D. Joseph]] and [[Thomas S. Lundgren]].<ref>Joseph, D. D., and T. S. Lundgren. "Quasilinear Dirichlet problems driven by positive sources." Archive for Rational Mechanics and Analysis 49.4 (1973): 241-269.</ref>

The solution for <math>n=1</math> that is valid in the range <math>\lambda \in [0,0.8785]</math> is given by

:<math>\psi = -2 \ln \left[e^{-\psi_m/2}\cosh \left(\frac{\sqrt{\lambda}}{\sqrt 2}e^{-\psi_m/2}r\right)\right]</math>

where <math>\psi_m=\psi(0)</math> is related to <math>\lambda</math> as

:<math>e^{\psi_m/2} = \cosh \left(\frac{\sqrt{\lambda}}{\sqrt 2}e^{-\psi_m/2}\right).</math>

The solution for <math>n=2</math> that is valid in the range <math>\lambda \in [0,2]</math> is given by

:<math>\psi = \ln \left[\frac{64e^{\psi_m}}{(\lambda  e^{\psi_m}r^2+8)^2}\right]</math>

where <math>\psi_m=\psi(0)</math> is related to <math>\lambda</math> as

:<math> (\lambda e^{\psi_m}+8)^2 - 64 e^{\psi_m} =0.</math>
